machatzit-hashekel/part-001.txt.1:ט: And on Shabbat on which 9th of Av falls, etc.—and there is practical difference at a mitzvah meal—meaning according to our custom explained in siman 551 that no person eats meat from Rosh Chodesh Av onward; if so what practical difference is there from this law—for we do not find according to us that one eats meat in the week in which 9th of Av falls; therefore he wrote there is practical difference at a mitzvah meal that falls in the week in which 9th of Av falls, that they are not permitted to eat meat except a limited meal and the rest eat dairy as written in siman 551 seif 10.
machatzit-hashekel/part-001.txt.1:י: After the beginning of the measure—that is, one hour per the custom Rama wrote in Yoreh Deah siman 89.
machatzit-hashekel/part-001.txt.1:כ: It should read birkat hamazon—before even waiting one hour as Rama wrote there.
machatzit-hashekel/part-001.txt.1:ל: The food will digest. And again he is not permitted to bless as above; and also there it means even if he waits six hours nevertheless he must bless birkat hamazon.
machatzit-hashekel/part-001.txt.2:א: (s.k. 2) From each other—and we do not say: since, etc. And their proof: if so the Talmud should also regarding terumah say the non-Kohen can ask about terumah—and they challenged in Avodat HaKodesh: for terumah in a Kohen's hand one does not ask as explained in Nedarim daf 59—see there. And one could say somewhat from that the Talmud teaches anonymously a Kohen eats terumah and did not explain what Israel gave him.
machatzit-hashekel/part-001.txt.2:ב: And if this Kohen separated terumah from his crop he can ask about it—it turns out the Gemara stated the inclusive reason even if Israel gave him terumah one cannot ask about it; even so he can invite zimun since the Kohen is permitted to eat with the Israelite. Nevertheless it must be said that he inferred from the Talmud's words: since a non-Kohen cannot eat terumah—it implies from its conclusion that an Israelite is not permitted to eat even terumah of the Kohen himself. And in any case it must be said that he inferred from the Talmud's language—for it told him the inclusive reason even for kodashim that one cannot ask about them when the sacrifice was already slaughtered.

magen-avraham/part-001.txt.3:א: Rabbeinu Yosef wrote the same regarding one who steals wheat and grinds and bakes—even though he acquired through change he does not bless neither at the beginning nor at the end; and so responsum 649; and so from the words of Rama siman 454 and siman 11 section 6; however in Rambam Laws of Matzah chapter 6 law 7 one does not fulfill with stolen matzah—this is the rule: anything one blesses birkat hamazon on one fulfills his obligation, and anything one does not bless birkat hamazon on one does not fulfill; and he wrote the same that if he acquired through change he fulfills—if so it is proven they bless birkat hamazon; and so one should instruct, for birkat hamazon is d'oraisa and we go stringently; and it is possible even one who stole bread blesses birkat hamazon, for when he ate it he already acquired through change; and further in siman 649 he was uncertain whether to bless; if so for birkat hamazon we hold stringently since it is d'oraisa as mentioned; and see chapter 6 of matzah in explanation of Yerushalmi—not like Bach. Cannot eat. It is difficult—for Yoreh Deah siman 112 chapter Darkei permits eating bread with them because of enmity; and one could say there specifically when they eat in one group enmity applies, but here each eats from his loaf—as is explicit there. Agudah wrote chapter 3 they ate: one eats cheese and two meat—they combine, for the cheese-eater can eat with the others; and so in Arakhin in the name of Semak; and so Rokeach laws of Berachot siman 334; and on Shabbat on which 9th of Av falls they do not invite zimun together those eating meat and those careful from meat and eating cheese, since none can eat with his fellow (Agudah chapter 4 of Taanit); and Hagah Maimoni challenged—for behold they can eat bread together, end of his words; and so Rashba on Semag explained they can invite zimun together; and it is difficult to be lenient against all these Geonim—one could say he holds they need to eat together that same bread his fellow eats—for otherwise Kohanim and non-Kohen could also eat other bread as Beit Yosef wrote in the name of Agur; rather we require that same bread, and here they cannot eat meat and cheese from one bread since it is soiled with meat as Yoreh Deah siman 89; and so Rokeach and Semak—they do not combine unless the cheese-eater can eat meat; and so Hagah Maimoni in the name of Maharash: two eat meat and one milk—the milk-eater blesses and discharges the other because he can eat with his fellow and not the reverse (gloss in small Mordechai, end of his words)—it implies specifically milk; but if he eats hard cheese they do not combine, for the custom now is not to eat meat after cheese; and on Shabbat on which 9th of Av falls even with milk they do not combine; and there is practical difference at a mitzvah meal; and from Hagah Maimoni's words it seems even if many they cannot invite zimun together, for one does not discharge his fellow and each group must invite zimun separately—and who will be lenient against all these great ones; and even Hagah Maimoni did not disagree but challenged them, and every difficulty has an answer; therefore one should not be lenient; and so is common speech. And I saw in Beit HaZevach beginning of Arakhin he challenged—for behold they can eat meat after waiting the measure; he was not precise—for in any case he must bless birkat hamazon first, and if he waits six hours the food digests; and also there it seems he must bless birkat hamazon first as Shach wrote in Yoreh Deah siman 89 in the name of Rashba.
magen-avraham/part-001.txt.3:ב: From each other. And we do not say: since if he wishes he can release his vow and they would combine.

mechaber/part-001.txt.1:main: One who ate a forbidden item—whether he combines for zimun. And in it are 4 seifim: One who ate a forbidden item—even though it is only d'rabbanan—one does not invite zimun upon him, and one does not bless on him neither at the beginning nor at the end.
mechaber/part-001.txt.2:main: If one ate a forbidden item in a place of danger, they bless on it. (And see below siman 204.)
mechaber/part-001.txt.3:main: Three who ate as one: one is careful from gentile bread and one is not careful, or one of them is a Kohen and eats challah—even though the careful one cannot eat with the one who is not careful, and an Israelite cannot with the Kohen—since the one who is not careful can eat with the careful one, and a Kohen with an Israelite, they combine. But if Kohanim and a non-Kohen ate as one and the Kohanim eat challah and are careful from gentile bread while the non-Kohen eats gentile bread—they do not combine. And the same applies to three who vowed benefit from each other that they do not combine for zimun. {Rama: And specifically when each eats from his own loaf; but if they eat from the host's loaf they combine, for behold they eat from one loaf (Avraham Zalman).}
mechaber/part-001.txt.4:main: One does not invite zimun upon one who ate less than a kezayit.

mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.1:א: (1) Forbidden item—even if its prohibition is not intrinsic but because he forbade this thing upon himself.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.1:ב: (2) And one does not bless on him—and the same applies one does not answer amen to his blessing.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.1:ג: (3) Not at the beginning, etc.—since it is a forbidden item and there is a transgression in eating it, he blasphemes Hashem in his blessing on this; and as it says: one who breaks a covenant blesses, blasphemes Hashem.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.1:ד: (4) And not at the end—and even if he ate to satiety; and if he ate b'shogeg and remembered after eating, the view of Taz and several Acharonim is that in this he may bless at the end (that is, even if he did not eat to satiety)—for here blasphemy is not applicable; but for zimun even b'shogeg one does not invite zimun on this, for eating forbidden food is not regarded as fixed eating. If he stole or robbed wheat and ground and baked—some say that even though he acquired through change and they are his, only that he owes him money for them, nevertheless it is forbidden to bless on this, both opening blessing and birkat hamazon—for regarding blessing which includes mention of the Name it is stricter and it is always in the category of blasphemy; and some say since he acquired he may bless; and the view of Magen Avraham is that for birkat hamazon if he ate to satiety one should instruct that he bless birkat hamazon, for it is d'oraisa, and one should be stringent and bless.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.2:א: (5) Forbidden item—even if he ate a d'oraisa prohibition in a place of danger such as due to illness; and the reason is since it is danger the Torah permitted him to eat, and on the contrary he fulfills a mitzvah to save his soul, as it is written "and live by them"—and they expounded "and live by them" and not die by them.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.2:ב: (6) And see below siman 204—where this law is repeated and explained there in Shulchan Aruch in the gloss that if they forced him to eat he does not bless, even though he was compelled to eat due to danger—and see there in Mishna Berurah.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.3:א: (7) They combine—even though each eats from his own loaf.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.3:ב: (8) They do not combine—for every combination for zimun is only when they can join together in their eating to eat one bread; and here each is careful from his fellow's bread.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.3:ג: (9) For three who vowed benefit from each other—whether each is under a vow from his fellow, or one is under a vow from the two and the two from him—for in any case that one cannot eat from theirs and they from his, therefore they do not combine; but when two are under a vow from one and he is not under a vow from them they certainly combine, since that one can eat with them. The poskim wrote the same when one eats milk or cheese and the two eat meat—they combine, for the cheese-eater can eat from their bread even though it is soiled with meat if he wipes his mouth and rinses (and the custom is that the cheese-eater is the one who blesses zimun and not the reverse, since he causes the zimun); but if he eats hard cheese they do not combine, for the custom now is not to eat meat after hard cheese even with wiping and rinsing; and similarly from Rosh Chodesh until 9th of Av they do not eat meat except at a mitzvah meal, and some are careful also in this and eat only dairy foods as written in siman 551—those careful from meat and eating dairy do not combine with meat-eaters, for behold they cannot eat with each other; unless they ate a kezayit of bread before the meat-eaters began eating meat in their bread—then they were still able to eat together; or if one of the members of the meal ate a kezayit of bread that is not soiled neither with meat nor milk—this combines everyone, for behold all can eat from his bread.

netiv-chayim/part-001.txt.1:_: (Magen Avraham s.k. 1) that they bless birkat hamazon on it, end of his words; and so one should instruct—as it should read.
netiv-chayim/part-001.txt.2:_: (there) And further in siman 649 Bach is uncertain in the name of Ran whether to bless; if so for birkat hamazon we hold stringently since it is d'oraisa—as it should read; and see the same in chapter 6 of matzah, etc.—as it should read. And it appears to me I do not understand—for if so with stolen matzah too one fulfills b'dieved, for he acquired through change; and proof from siman 649 is nothing—for there he acquired through change without support of the mitzvah, unlike here where the change comes through support of the mitzvah and it is mitzvah coming through transgression; and according to everyone one does not bless—and understand well.

peri-megadim/part-001.txt.1:א: But Taz brought the words of Ramah and R' Eliezer of Metz chapter 1 of Berachot law 19; and for R' Eliezer of Metz who blesses before—it is difficult from Berachot 43b that on incense of idolatry one does not bless; and one must say regarding d'oraisa prohibition Ramah agrees one does not bless—for his main proof is from chapter 3 "they ate" 45a tevel—for d'rabbanan one does not invite zimun, they bless; and on incense of forbidden relations which is forbidden to smell d'rabbanan—likewise one blesses according to R' Eliezer of Metz; and so wrote Malbim there that what Ramah wrote chapter 9 of Berachot law 8 one does not bless on incense of forbidden relations—for his reason he goes; but for R' Eliezer of Metz on gentile incense which is d'oraisa one does not bless, and of forbidden relations d'rabbanan one blesses. And in the margin it is written see R' Yehuda siman 65; but for what Taz wrote R' Eliezer of Metz disagrees only b'shogeg or in danger—it implies Ramah holds even in danger he does not bless; and for R' Eliezer of Metz in danger he blesses beginning and end. And one could say what Taz wrote for Ramah—it teaches zimun, for zimun is worse than fruits—for Ramah in chapter 8 law 8 of Berachot for three fruits do not combine; and so the Mechaber in siman 197 and Beit Yosef siman 71; and in several places he also explained 71—see there; and I return to Taz's intent: what he wrote Mishnah 3 "they ate," etc.—deals with b'shogeg—for b'mezid he is wicked—one could say what of it, since they did not excommunicate him they invite zimun upon him as in siman 199 seif 1 and siman 55—see there; and his general rule is that for Ramah b'shogeg and danger are one; and proof from responsum Rashba that for Ramah a sick person on Yom Kippur does not bless (and how much more one who eats forbidden food in danger of life—he does not bless for Ramah); and Ramah's proof from Mishnah one ate tevel—for d'rabbanan one does not invite zimun even b'shogeg—and he holds the reason is because it is not regarded as eating at all; the same applies he does not bless; and R' Eliezer of Metz holds specifically zimun no, for there is no fixed eating and it is like fruits (and he holds for three fruits not like Ramah chapter 5 law 8); and Rosh agreed with R' Eliezer b'shogeg—and the same in danger; and one could say what R' Eliezer wrote he blesses at the beginning—in danger it refers; and Rosh agreed with R' Eliezer b'shogeg he blesses at the end, and danger even at the beginning; and one does not invite zimun—for it is worse than eating fruits (as siman 199 for Rosh); and proof that he explained blasphemy—that b'shogeg and danger there is no blasphemy. And the Mechaber here ruled like Ramah that one does not bless; and nevertheless he ruled danger one blesses—he holds to distinguish between b'shogeg who regrets and it is not regarded as significant eating, unlike danger—see Sefer Chemed Moshe. But nevertheless it is puzzling why the Mechaber omitted b'shogeg. And from responsum Rashba one could say he says preferentially that in any case there is permission at the forbidden hour Ramah agrees; and if not, in Magen Avraham it will be explained further here; and here one should not expand.
peri-megadim/part-001.txt.1:ב: If he ate doubtful d'oraisa prohibition he does not bless—for if it were certain d'rabbanan he would not bless; and what is doubtful d'oraisa for stringency.
peri-megadim/part-001.txt.1:ג: And if three ate forbidden food in danger, or one of them—one does not invite zimun upon him; and so from Shulchan Aruch that they bless and he did not write they invite zimun too; so too in our chiddushim beginning of chapter 3 "they ate"; and that which it does not answer tevel—it is obvious in danger he speaks truth even d'rabbanan no. And demai—specifically they invite zimun upon him; other things like challah of an am ha'aretz some say are nullified in the majority—nevertheless now it is forbidden he ate.
peri-megadim/part-001.txt.2:_: And the non-Kohen—Taz in Arakhin 2: Kohanim, Levites, and Israelites are obligated in zimun—lest you say a non-Kohen does not eat terumah and kodashim, Kohanim can eat with a non-Kohen—if not; and Taz added that it is not d'oraisa that it is possible through asking; and it may be it refers to three under vows of benefit—and see Tosafot Arakhin 3a who wrote terumah one can ask; and that is after it came to a Kohen's hand. Again I saw in Avodat HaKodesh part 2 chapter 2 siman 7 they raised this from Gemara Nedarim 59a—and requires study.
peri-megadim/part-001.txt.3:_: If—Taz Yoreh Deah 112 siman 65 and Eshel Avraham there.
peri-megadim/part-001.txt.4:_: One does not—Taz Rashi Berachot 45a; and perhaps it is difficult for him—for zimun even only with three as siman 199 for Rosh; therefore he said to discharge others one needs specifically a kezayit of bread—or otherwise one would say in any case he blesses birkat hamazon—and what difference is zimun? Therefore he explained thus; and if so it is difficult on the Mechaber—for in siman 199 seif 2 he wrote the blesser should be one of the bread-eaters; and in siman 484 seif 6 he wrote the measure of birkat hamazon is a kezayit; and one could say the Mechaber explains simply—in any case one invites zimun on a kezayit; for d'oraisa to combine for zimun even less than a kezayit of bread also combines—it teaches us.

rabbi-akiva-eiger/part-001.txt.1:_: s.k. 1—one who ate a forbidden item. And if he ate bread kneaded in milk or forbidden fat lest he come to eat it with meat—one could say it is not so called forbidden; and especially for what Knesset HaGedolah wrote in siman 197 that one may divide the bread for blessing only in a matter where each has a small amount—if so one could say it is like demai that they bless, since if he wishes he declares his property ownerless and eats b'heter; the same here if he wishes he divides and eats a kezayit b'heter—and see Eshel Avraham siman 168 s.k. 16.
rabbi-akiva-eiger/part-001.txt.2:_: Magen Avraham s.k. 1—neither at beginning nor end. See responsum Bach part 2 siman 1.

shaarei-teshuvah/part-001.txt.1:_: At the end—see Baer Heitev; and see in responsum Bach Chadashot who also raised to bless at the end and it is not blasphemy even though there is a mitzvah; and in another fascicle he wrote there, and in the gloss under the name of a great one regarding one who vowed or swore not to eat a certain thing and transgressed and ate—he is obligated to bless at the end; but at the beginning when he wishes to eat—for at the time of blessing he wishes to do a prohibition in any case—he should not bless, end of his words. And what Baer Heitev wrote in the name of responsum Be'er Eshek—see Eshel Avraham from responsa Beit Yehudah, and it is in Yoreh Deah siman 23; and see Halakhot Ketanot part 1 and She'elat Yaavetz siman 45; and see responsum Beit Efrayim part 1 siman 63 inside explaining the aggadah in Shabbat daf 139 from the day Yosef separated from his brothers, etc.—see there. And see at the end of responsum Tashbetz in the third Tur siman 29; and see in Beit Yosef in the name of Maharshal who wrote in his glosses from Sefer Zichron Moshe that amen and zimun blessing are equal, and one does not answer after one who blessed on eating a forbidden item as Tosafot on demai; but when it is something the eater permits himself and the listener forbids—such as gentile bread and similar—the listeners may answer amen after him, for this is not blasphemy at all like zimun where they invite zimun upon one not careful from gentile bread, end of his words.
shaarei-teshuvah/part-001.txt.2:_: Danger—see Baer Heitev; and see in Peri Megadim part 2 siman 7 that his intent is to rule like Rambam that forbidden food when a person's soul is at an end—even b'shogeg or for healing even afterward he is not obligated to bless, for it is not regarded as benefit—see there; and see Pesachim daf 107 in Tosafot s.v. there are two types of coarse eating—see there; and see below siman 204 what is written there.
shaarei-teshuvah/part-001.txt.3:_: They combine—see Baer Heitev; and what he wrote in the name of Magen Avraham that they cannot eat the bread soiled with meat—he challenged this in the place of Shmuel siman 94—for behold he can eat after he finishes eating milk; and even in the week in which 9th of Av falls it is permitted in a meat dish; if so he is not forbidden from that bread—and see there that nevertheless he concludes it is preferable not to combine for zimun on Shabbat on which 9th of Av falls, meat-eaters with dairy-eaters—see there; and see siman 135 on what Shulchan Aruch and Tur wrote regarding three who measure benefit from each other on Beit Yosef's words who brought proof from that it was necessary to say Kohanim eat ordinary food—teach us that if he wishes he can compromise, etc.; and he challenged that for terumah in a Kohen's hand he cannot compromise—see there; and see inside Me'orot part 2 siman 6 who challenged thus and wrote to resolve somewhat—see there; and so Peri Chadash in Likutim wrote to resolve somewhat; and see Avodat HaKodesh and Gan siman 80 and Beit Yosef—see there; and see Yad Ephraim in the name of Beit Yosef regarding one who swore not to speak with his fellow—he is not permitted to invite zimun upon him; and what is written there regarding the law if there are ten in zimun what is his law—see there.

turei-zahav/part-001.txt.1:_: One who ate a forbidden item. So wrote Rambam chapter 1 of Berachot; and Raavad challenged him and said thus: He erred in this—for they only said there is no zimun upon them to say they have no significance of fixed eating since they eat a forbidden item like eating fruits that have no fixed eating for zimun; but an opening and closing blessing—why should they not bless, since he benefits, end of his words—and this is from the Mishnah at the beginning of chapter 3 "they ate": one ate tevel—even d'rabbanan one does not invite zimun upon him; and Raavad holds specifically for zimun no, but blessers we bless; and Rambam must hold they taught zimun as a leniency, for it is lighter than birkat hamazon—for even on a vegetable leaf one of them ate we invite zimun—it teaches that forbidden food is worse; all the more so he does not bless; and Rosh agreed with Raavad—from that which is in chapter HaGozel: R' Meir said one who stole a se'ah of wheat, ground, kneaded, baked, and separated challah—how does he bless? This one does not bless but blasphemes; and on this it says one who breaks a covenant blesses, blasphemes Hashem—behold he is obligated to bless only his blessing is blasphemy, end of his words; and Beit Yosef strengthened Rambam's view from Yerushalmi stolen matzah forbidden to bless on it, etc.; and further from Tosefta: on all of these one does not bless and one does not invite zimun, etc.; and that which "this one does not bless but blasphemes" means therefore he should not bless; and in my humble opinion certainly Rosh did not bring proof from blasphemy to learn that he should bless and blaspheme God—for silence is certainly better for him; rather it seems Raavad too does not disagree on one who eats forbidden food b'mezid but on b'shogeg—as Rambam wrote there: anyone who eats forbidden food whether intentionally or unwittingly does not bless beginning or end, etc.; and it appears to me all hold the Mishnah that said one ate tevel one does not invite zimun means he ate b'shogeg—for b'mezid he would be completely wicked and obviously one does not invite zimun with him; rather certainly b'shogeg we say thus; and Rambam holds his eating is not regarded as eating at all and similar to what is written in Yoreh Deah siman 119 one who sells to his fellow something forbidden d'oraisa and he ate—they return the money, for it is as if he did not eat; so too for blessing, and stricter—for even d'rabbanan prohibition regarding blessing it is as if he did not eat at all; and from this reason it seems one who eats forbidden food at a time of danger does not bless for Rambam—for one reason is who understands his error, and it is retroactively as if he ate permitted; nevertheless he does not bless; and so Beit Yosef afterward in the name of Mahari Weil. And although Beit Yosef wrote it seems Rambam agrees that in all such cases he blesses, etc.—very puzzling why b'shogeg should be worse than time of danger like b'mezid—for there too there is coercion in b'shogeg, for his heart coerced him, for he is exempt from punishment of oath if he swore falsely as explained in Shevuot in the students of Rav for the reason "the person in the oath" except one compelled; and similarly a woman who committed adultery b'shogeg is like one compelled; rather it appears plain to my humble opinion that the essence is as Mahari Weil wrote—even at time of danger he does not bless for Rambam; and so from responsum Rashba siman 494 regarding a sick person who eats on Yom Kippur he ruled he must bless and wrote: although Rambam ruled on one who ate tevel he does not bless—but from where does he have it, and Raavad challenged him, end of his words—behold he equated this law of eating tevel to a sick person on Yom Kippur and certainly b'shogeg is dealt with and he compares to one compelled like a sick person—and in both Raavad disagrees that b'shogeg he blesses since he benefits, only one does not invite zimun upon him for his eating is not regarded as fixed eating; but for blessing beginning and end he blesses since he benefited; and although b'shogeg opening blessing is not applicable—for he did not know there is a prohibition here—nevertheless opening blessing applies where he is compelled, for that too is called b'shogeg even though he acts b'mezid; if so Rosh agrees well with Raavad's words from that which we say this one does not bless but blasphemes—it implies blessing applies only he blasphemes, and that is b'mezid; but if he did so b'shogeg there is no blasphemy; if so the obligation of blessing remains upon him properly; and what Beit Yosef brought proof from forbidden to bless from stolen matzah—and so Tosafot—that deals with b'mezid and there is no proof for b'shogeg; also Rabbeinu Tur's words can be explained on b'shogeg as to my humble opinion correctly; and even if you say Raavad and Rosh are not explained thus, nevertheless for the law it appears proper to rule that one who eats forbidden food b'shogeg blesses afterward, since he already ruled in danger one must bless—and certainly they are one matter; see responsum Rashba siman 497.
turei-zahav/part-001.txt.2:_: And the non-Kohen eats bread, etc. Beit Yosef brought Agur's words here that they combine since if it happened at their meal with ordinary bread of Israel they can eat together; and he wrote on this they are idle words from that in Eruvin, end of his words—and this is from that which we say regarding terumah they do not combine, and although it is possible through asking, nevertheless behold it was not yet asked; and it appears to me if bread of Israel is available and ready, even though they did not eat from it, nevertheless it is possible for them to eat together from it and they combine; and with this Beit Yosef agrees; only it is difficult from what is said in the next siman in Shulchan Aruch—that is, what is said in the Gemara: Rav and Shmuel were sitting at a meal; Rav Shimi came hurrying to eat with them in order to combine with them for zimun; he said to him: what is your thinking to combine with us—you already ate. Shmuel said: if these bring appetizers to father would he not eat. And Rif explained: wherever if they bring something he could eat from it he combines with them, end of his words; and if so a fortiori—there where they were not yet obligated in zimun at all, nevertheless since it is possible to say if they bring something they would eat from this reasoning to obligate zimun—a fortiori here where all ate, only one cannot eat with his fellow—it is obvious this reasoning helps that if bread of Israel happens to them that he can eat one with his fellow and they combine for zimun.
turei-zahav/part-001.txt.3:_: If they eat from the host's loaf. Yoreh Deah siman 221 is explained that it is forbidden for them to eat in one bowl lest one eat from his fellow's portion unless the gentile's custom is to return and fill one bowl after they ate—or it is permitted; if so here too it necessarily deals with this custom.
turei-zahav/part-001.txt.4:_: One does not invite zimun, etc. In the Mishnah they say: until where does one invite zimun? Until a kezayit. Rashi explained: how much should he eat with them and become obligated with them in zimun; and there is practical difference to discharge them if they give him the cup to bless, end of his words; and if so this is what is written afterward siman 199 that the blesser should be one of the bread-eaters.

yad-ephraim/part-001.txt.1:_: In Magen Avraham beginning of siman—he fulfills with it—as it should read.
yad-ephraim/part-001.txt.2:_: There—and it is possible even one who stole bread, etc. See in responsum Bach Chadashot and in another fascicle there I wrote on these words of Magen Avraham—it appears he means from its essence he acquired; and I brought there from the words of Ritva in Sukkah daf 35—see there.
yad-ephraim/part-001.txt.3:_: In Magen Avraham s.k. 2—and we do not say since if he wishes he releases his vow, etc. And see in Beit Yosef in the name of Mahari Prague in responsum manuscript: Reuven swore not to speak with Shimon and they ate together with another—Reuven is not permitted to invite zimun, for he speaks with both of them and tells them to be ready for the blessing, end of his words—and requires study; and therefore if Reuven wants to be shaliach tzibur to say Barchu when Shimon is in synagogue, especially if there are not ten except by combining Shimon—for all of them he tells to bless and Shimon is included—here too it is forbidden; and one could distinguish since there is a majority who are not offended he can speak to them; and Shimon should combine only to answer alone, for there is no matter of sanctity in fewer than ten; but according to this reasoning here too there is room to permit if the diners are many—and requires study; also requires study on the essence of the law that one swore not to speak with Shimon—one could say the intent is only not to speak with him alone privately, but generally when he speaks to many and he too is included it is not in the vow; and see Yoreh Deah siman 221 that Rambam wrote one may speak with another and he hears. But in responsum of the Geonim that Beit Yosef brought it is explained that if he intended to make him hear even though another is between them—his words are toward that person—Reuven does not act properly; and even according to what the Geonim wrote there initially, nevertheless they required the agent to say to Shimon what Reuven says through the agent and not rely on Reuven because Shimon heard his words from his mouth when he said to the agent speak to Shimon thus and so—meaning even though Shimon heard in Reuven's telling the agent that he should speak to Shimon thus, nevertheless the agent must repeat the words to Shimon so it appears Reuven does not rely on Shimon's hearing from his mouth what he said to the agent; and Rambam's words that came in general one may speak with another and he hears—requires study; and it is possible he holds what the Geonim wrote that the agent speaks, etc., for clarity of the matter, but there is no strictness in this, and whenever he does not speak with him face to face it is not in the vow; and from Shach there who cited from responsum of the Geonim what he wrote that if he intended to make him hear he does not act properly—it implies he explains Rambam's words too that he should not intend to make him hear; and from Rambam's language it does not imply so. But nevertheless even though we say intending to make him hear is forbidden—there is no proof for this law, for there he need not speak with the other, only another mediates between them and the essence of speech is directed to the one he swore about; unlike here where the essence of speech is not directed to him but to many, and even though he too is included in the speech—one could say he did not swear except not to speak with so-and-so alone, but not among other people—and requires study for now. And behold from responsum of the Geonim it is proven explicitly that one who swore not to speak with his fellow is permitted to speak with him through an agent—and we do not say one's agent is like oneself; and it must be these are words and there is no law of agency; and one can give a reason according to what Tosafot R' Yehuda wrote that mitzvot on one's body literally have no law of agency; and I expanded elsewhere; and see what is written in responsum part Choshen Mishpat and in the laws of Kaddish for an orphan I expanded further—see there.
